planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil with light shade from the hottest afternoon sun to protect the variegated margins; Marginata needs only infrequent light shearing to stay dense.

directions: Marginata is one of the oldest named variegated boxwood forms, with silvery white-margined foliage first noted in English gardening literature in John Parkinson's 1629 Paradisi in Sole Paradisus Terrestris, well before most modern variegated selections were developed. It grows as a slow, dense, rounded shrub much like unvariegated English boxwood, but the pale leaf edges give it a lighter, almost frosted appearance useful for brightening dark corners or mixed borders. Because the margin is a true leaf-pigment variegation rather than a sport prone to reverting quickly, plants hold their pattern reliably for many years with routine light shearing. Give it the same well-drained, humus-rich soil and some afternoon shade that other English boxwood selections prefer, since strong variegation can scorch in intense summer sun.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil, siting it well away from structures and paths to accommodate its eventual tree-like size.

directions: Arborescens is a larger-growing common boxwood selection, developing over many decades into a more tree-like form rather than the low mounded shrub most people picture when they hear 'boxwood.' Its leaves run noticeably larger and more elongated than typical English boxwood foliage, giving mature plants a coarser, bolder texture at a distance. Growers use it for tall screening hedges, large-scale topiary, or as a clipped or naturalistic small specimen tree where standard boxwood cultivars would stay far too low. Because ultimate size is substantial, give it plenty of room from buildings and walkways and expect growth measured in many years rather than seasons.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil, staking young plants to a single leader if some height before the weeping habit develops is desired.

directions: Unraveled breaks from the tightly mounded habit typical of Japanese boxwood, instead sending out long, lax branches that cascade outward and downward as the plant ages, as though the usual dense boxwood form has come undone. Staking a young plant to a single leader lets growers build some height before the weeping character takes over, after which the arching branches can spread considerably wider than the plant is tall. Its small, glossy evergreen leaves keep the familiar boxwood texture and color even though the silhouette is anything but typical. Use it as a specimen, trained espalier, or cascading accent over a wall or large container where its unusual draping form can be fully appreciated.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil with good air movement around the foliage to support its bred-in blight resistance.

directions: Heritage is one of two patented releases in the BetterBoxwood line, a group of European hybrids bred and trialed for improved resistance to boxwood blight. It grows taller than it is wide, building a dense, upright form of dark green foliage that closely resembles classic American boxwood in color and texture. Because the breeding targeted disease resistance rather than extreme dwarfing, plants reach a modest, manageable hedge or foundation-planting size without the slow multi-decade wait typical of heirloom English boxwood selections. Space plants for a tight formal hedge or use singly as a narrow accent, and give it well-drained soil with good air circulation to keep its bred-in blight resistance working in its favor.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil, allowing enough lateral room for its wider-than-tall mature spread.

directions: Renaissance is the companion patented release to Heritage in the BetterBoxwood breeding line, selected from the same European blight-resistance trials but shaped as a wider-than-tall, almost groundcover-like mound rather than an upright form. Its lighter green foliage reads noticeably softer than the darker leaves typical of American or English boxwood, giving plantings a slightly different tone when mixed with older cultivars. The spreading habit suits low foundation plantings, broad edging, or massed groupings where a wide, low evergreen presence is wanted without aggressive shearing. As with other blight-resistant hybrids, well-drained soil and good airflow help the plant's natural disease tolerance perform at its best.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

common_name: Liberty Belle Boxwood (Low-Spreading NewGen Hybrid Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; because growth is very slow, expect this low mound to take many years to fill in completely.

directions: Liberty Belle is a low, wider-than-tall selection from the NewGen boxwood breeding program bred by Robert Head, the same disease-resistance effort that produced NewGen Independence and NewGen Freedom, but bred and trialed specifically for a smaller, more spreading habit. Growth is notably slow even by boxwood standards, so the plant holds a tidy low mound with minimal pruning for years after planting. Like its NewGen siblings it carries improved resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer, making it a lower-maintenance option where older Korean or English boxwood selections have struggled with disease. Its modest height suits low edging, foundation plantings, or the front of a mixed border where a dependable, slow, disease-resistant evergreen is needed.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
